title: A Financial Regime Shift Is Coming - Systematic Investor 332

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/A Financial Regime Shift Is Coming - Systematic Investor 332.docx

speakers: Mark (guest, quantitative macro researcher and professor, Boston)
Alan Dunne (guest host, Top Traders Unplugged)
summary: Top Traders Unplugged with Mark: January 2025 regime shift with record policy uncertainty but a quiet VIX, and the split between measurable risk (volatility) and non-measurable uncertainty. Mark argues trend following and flexible beta suit regime change, convergent multistrat strategies carry hidden risk, and models should be stress-tested on uncertainty spikes.

completeness_estimate: 0.88 - first reader caught the core mechanisms; missed VVIX data, the lagged-correlation forecast, the new-administration starting conditions, monetary-policy uncertainty as a term-premium source, the analogue-data caveat and the leverage-caution conclusion

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: there are a number of uncertainty indices that have been available
claims.claim: Policy/economic uncertainty indices give a number for how large a regime change is, which is how a quantitative investor can measure the Biden-to-Trump shift.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: what they do is that they measure the word uncertainty under certain newspapers
claims.claim: Newspaper-text-based uncertainty indices (Stanford economic policy uncertainty family; monetary, trade, general policy) count uncertainty words on a rolling one-month basis.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we have the world uncertainty in indic has has spiked to levels that we haven't seen since 2020
claims.claim: In January 2025 world uncertainty hit its highest level since 2020, with US uncertainty above European uncertainty (unusual).

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: when uncertainty has a shock you're going to get uh lower investment you're going to have lower consumption
claims.claim: An uncertainty shock lowers investment and consumption because firms delay projects, slowing financial and real activity.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: this actually creates Trends because everything is slowed down and what happens it also creates more expectation dispersion
claims.claim: Higher uncertainty creates trends (slowed adjustment) and widens dispersion of expectations.
claims.testable: partly - need link uncertainty to trend-following returns

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we have policy uncertainty we have Global uncertainty but we don't have vix uncertainty
claims.claim: In early 2025 the VIX stayed below 20 despite record uncertainty indices, so implied volatility was not pricing the uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: one could be what is measurable and uh we'll call it measurable risk would be volatility
claims.claim: Risk has a measurable part (volatility) and a non-measurable part (uncertainty); volatility alone understates risk when uncertainty is high.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we have relatively stable measurable volatility right now but we have very high non-measurable uncertainty
claims.claim: Early 2025: stable volatility but very high uncertainty means true risk is higher than volatility indicates.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: higher uncertainty actually uh leads to differences in Behavior
claims.claim: High uncertainty raises the chance of changes in trends and in cross-market relationships.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: a Quant loves everything that's measurable so they they hate the fact that there is high uncertainty
claims.claim: Quant models struggle with high uncertainty while discretionary traders see more opportunity from their subjective views.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if you get the regime change quote unquote wrong or you don't see it coming that's probably where you're going to have the biggest you know potential for loss
claims.claim: Missing a regime change causes the biggest losses because of excess leverage, under-diversification, wrong correlations and missed trends, so measure regime change to rebalance risk.
claims.direction: reduce risk when volatility/correlation regime shifts

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: that's going to have an impact on your overall volatility in your 640 you know allocation
claims.claim: A regime change with higher equity and bond volatility raises the volatility of a 60/40 allocation.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: when we had a higher inflation we saw that there was an increase in in the stock Bond correlation it went positive
claims.claim: The stock-bond correlation turns positive when inflation is high, so inflation regime determines whether bonds hedge equities.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we expect that there's going to be a breakdown and correlation across countries and Market
claims.claim: Tariffs and changing trade flows (less US trade, more intra-Asia) should break down cross-country correlations, ending the globalisation-driven connectedness.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: what we should sort of see is is that Arbitrage pricing
claims.claim: Tariffs on imported metals (copper, zinc, lead, steel) should show up as US-versus-London futures contract price gaps equal to the tariff.
claims.indicator: US vs LME copper, zinc, lead futures spread
claims.direction: US price above London by tariff

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: some managers will adjust their correlations on a on a calendar basis
claims.claim: Managers recalibrate correlation matrices on a fixed calendar (e.g. six months) while position sizing uses short-term volatility, so regime changes enter risk estimates with a lag; shorten the update period.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: stockchain CTA up 0.26% sock gen Trend um now is down 0.69% on the month
claims.claim: Late January 2025: SG CTA +0.26%, SG Trend -0.69% on the month, with the dollar up early then falling bond markets reversing, i.e. choppy.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we've gone for a long period of time in the uh we'll call it the QE period of no term premium
claims.claim: During QE bonds had no term premium and hedged equities; with QE ended and rising term premium the hedge role is less reliable.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: she has some concerns about the size of deficit so the possibility of of crowding out
claims.claim: Large deficits raise the possibility of crowding out, which adds term premium to long bonds.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you're really looking at what's the growth rate plus expected inflation and that's your is your quick proxy for what is the fair value for bonds
claims.claim: Bond fair value is growth plus expected inflation plus a risk premium; omitting the premium predicts bond rallies that may not occur.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you had more growth uncertainty there might be a bias to be more biased towards owning bonds whereas kind of inflation uncertainty maybe less so
claims.claim: Growth uncertainty favours owning bonds while inflation uncertainty does not; separate uncertainty indices (trade, monetary, policy) exist.
claims.direction: growth uncertainty: long bonds; inflation uncertainty: not
claims.testable: yes - regress bond returns on type-specific indices

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: there always is a disconnect between what is Promised versus what is actually delivered
claims.claim: Handicap political promises against actual delivery; new-administration uncertainty resolves and re-creates itself as policy is implemented.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: should would be stagflationary in the sense that if you don't have as many workers people can't you can't hire
claims.claim: Cutting immigration shrinks labour supply, lowering payroll growth and potential growth while pushing up wages, which is stagflationary.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: it's going to be the growth in population and and and your productivity
claims.claim: Long-term growth equals population growth plus productivity growth, so a declining working-age population needs productivity gains.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: economic growth you know the economy is determined by the set of Institutions and the interactions between agents within the economy
claims.claim: New institutional economics: growth depends on institutions, including labour force composition, not just worker counts.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: once they add in transactions cost is is that there was a what was positive Alpha strategies depending on the size of the portfolio almost went negative
claims.claim: A recent paper on long-only trend following in equities found positive alpha almost vanished after transaction costs, depending on portfolio size, so institutional frictions must be modelled.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we can go back and take any model and be able to sort of say well what was the performance like when there was a spike in uncertainty
claims.claim: Stress-test any model by its performance in past uncertainty-index spikes to bracket expected performance and understand why it works or fails.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: depending on your time frame for your model you either actually sort of came out okay
claims.claim: In the Feb-May 2020 uncertainty spike, short- and long-horizon models differed: some made money while others got badly hurt, depending on time horizon.
claims.indicator: model time horizon in uncertainty spike (2020)

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we went back over the periods of high uncertainty and here's how our model performed
claims.claim: Allocators value managers who disclose performance in high-uncertainty periods to bracket expectations without claiming history will repeat.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we went off the gold standard is it who would have thought that that would have happened and then that changed the regime you know significantly
claims.claim: Regime breaks (end of Bretton Woods 1971, rate spikes in 1980, 1992 EMS failure, euro) were not anticipated, so be aware anything is possible.

correction.issue: Most examples (double-digit rates under Carter, Plaza Accord, 1992 EMS break, the euro) are spoken in C11; only Bretton Woods 1971 is in C10, and the rate spike is 'end of the Carter administration' rather than 1980 specifically.
correction.fix: Regime breaks such as the end of Bretton Woods (1971), double-digit rates at the end of the Carter administration, the Plaza Accord, the 1992 EMS break and the euro were not anticipated, so models should allow that anything is possible.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: there's been a tremendous amount of resilience
claims.claim: After each regime break markets and the world survived.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: the trend following is actually a good strategy to increase exposure to under regime change because one is this is that it's not really making a lot of assumptions or forecasts
claims.claim: Trend following makes no mean-reversion assumptions, so it suits regime change, unlike carry or long/short equity that rely on stable linkages.
claims.indicator: trend following vs carry and long/short equity
claims.conditions: During regime change and high uncertainty

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we could think of trend following as more antifragile okay
claims.claim: Trend following is antifragile (Taleb) because it only buys what is rising and sells what falls; in high uncertainty it should do better.
claims.testable: partly - uncertainty index vs trend returns

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: what you want to have is a strategy that has a flexible overall beta relative to the stock market
claims.claim: Beta flex: hold flexible equity beta, higher when the market rises and negative when it falls, which means convexity.
claims.direction: long beta in uptrends, short in downtrends

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the types of strategies that people were increasing allocations for were the multi-manager multi strats uh stat ARB and and Quant multistat
claims.claim: An early-2025 bank survey showed investors adding to multi-managers, stat arb and quant multistrats and cutting credit long/short.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if we have a regime change what we're saying is that we don't really know what the equilibrium level is so consequently it's hard to move back to something that we can't measure
claims.claim: Convergent strategies assume a known equilibrium; in a regime change the equilibrium (e.g. term premium, inflation target) is uncertain, so mean reversion fails.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if we have an increase in tariffs you might have a situation that inflation could maybe be stickier at current levels
claims.claim: Tariffs plus the last-mile inflation problem could keep inflation sticky or higher, making bond valuations harder.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: the more I put into multistat the more I'm actually making a a a convergent mean reversion play
claims.claim: Multi-strategy platforms select high-Sharpe trades and lever them, which is structurally convergent and cannot hold volatile divergent strategies like trend following.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you can't you can't have a Divergent strategy and have a low volatility approach
claims.claim: Divergent strategies have higher volatility and lumpy returns with long quiet periods followed by concentrated gains in dislocations.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: the idea that I'm getting a paid liquidity premium for private equity fact that I get to get excess return versus public markets has not been the case
claims.claim: Private equity has not delivered excess returns over public equities on rolling windows, its low volatility comes from infrequent marking, and exits need a working IPO market.
claims.indicator: private equity vs public equity returns

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: it requires a rethinking of liquid versus illiquid strategies
claims.claim: Liquid strategies deserve reconsideration, since marking to market gives higher volatility but preserves liquidity without lower returns.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: they'll they'll throw as much money as they can until they until they can't
claims.claim: Banks lend increasing leverage to multi-strategy managers because positions are transparent via prime brokerage, creating a risk of a funding squeeze as in August 2024 carry unwind.
claims.conditions: If bank balance sheets are stressed

correction.issue: Overstates: Mark does not describe August 2024 as a bank funding squeeze; he lists the August 2024 carry unwind, the prior year's long-short problem and Mag 7 drawdowns as examples of existential risks for leveraged multistrat books.
correction.fix: Banks keep extending leverage to multi-strategy managers because prime-broker position transparency makes it easy, but episodes like the August 2024 carry unwind or Mag 7 drawdowns show these leveraged books face existential risks.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: they also have to make assumptions about what is the correlations and and what are the linkages across this
claims.claim: Prime broker risk models measure volatility well but depend on assumed correlations; the non-measurable uncertainty is what breaks leveraged books (carry unwind, Mag 7 losses).

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: complex system is is that usually have nonlinear response to different shocks
claims.claim: Complex systems have nonlinear shock responses and contagion, so ask whether models handle nonlinearity and what happens if correlations go to one.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: they've never been able to get uh be embraced by a lot of Traders or modelers in a very systematic fashion
claims.claim: Complexity theory (Santa Fe Institute) has not been turned into systematic trading models.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: what happens if correlations do go to one what do you do in your model
claims.claim: Due diligence question: how does the model respond when correlations go to one.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: the world of 15 years ago is not the same as it is today
claims.claim: Equal-weighting 20 years of history is questionable because the market rules and structure change; weight recent data differently.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if there's less you know uh pages in the Federal Register which is the amount of regul ations that occur that actually small cap stocks will do better
claims.claim: Less regulation (fewer Federal Register pages) helps small caps because compliance has a higher fixed cost for small firms (Laffer and Canto).
claims.indicator: Federal Register page count vs small-cap performance
claims.direction: long small caps when regulation falls

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: depending on like what is the amount of reverse repo that you do at the Fed all of a sudden that has a big impact on money markets
claims.claim: Reversing QE has unmodelled effects, such as reverse repo changing money-market flows; think through such second-order policy effects.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if you look at the vix which is the volatility of the vix the last six months have been elevated versus the first six months of 2024 but we're we're still sort of saying we haven't seen a spike
claims.claim: Volatility-of-volatility (VVIX) was elevated in the second half of 2024 versus the first half even though VIX itself stayed range-bound, with only a brief spike around the December 2024 Fed meeting.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you're not going to see it right away because in in the in the first week we haven't seen the spike in and vix but we should sort of see over the next three months
claims.claim: A policy regime change shows up in realised cross-market correlations with a lag: not in the first week, but over roughly the next three months, so correlation estimates updated only periodically will be late.
claims.indicator: rolling cross-market correlations after a regime shift
claims.direction: correlations shift over ~3 months after the shock
claims.testable: yes - correlation change after uncertainty spikes

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we're at the low end of unemployment we're probably in the uh uh you know mid to slightly lower end of real GDP so there's more room for growth uh economic utilization is at at the high levels
claims.claim: Compared with conditions at the start of past presidential terms, January 2025 had low unemployment, mid-to-low real GDP growth, high utilisation, slightly elevated core inflation and poor debt/GDP, so the room for further improvement (and for the euphoric outlook) is limited.
claims.indicator: unemployment, real GDP growth, capacity utilisation, core inflation, debt/GDP at inauguration

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if you also have high mon AR policy uncertainty and uh I think that there's a view that maybe September was uh was uh overly aggressive
claims.claim: Bond term premium is being pushed up by both growth uncertainty and monetary-policy uncertainty, the latter because the September 2024 Fed cut may have been too aggressive and the Fed path is unclear.
claims.indicator: monetary policy uncertainty index, term premium
claims.testable: yes - MPU index vs term premium

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: well it's hard to get robust information on there and then and that's where the institutional differences uh have have an impact
claims.claim: Building hypothetical stress data from distant analogues such as the 1930s trade wars is not robust, because data are poor and institutions differed; better to accept that anything is possible.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: would this be the best time to increase leverage lending to these Institution you might be a little bit uh you want give this a little bit
claims.claim: When non-measurable uncertainty is high, linkages, volatility and dislocations can change unexpectedly, so it is a poor time for banks to extend more leverage to multi-strategy funds.
claims.indicator: uncertainty indices, prime-broker leverage to multistrats
claims.direction: reduce leverage provision when uncertainty is high
claims.testable: partly - deleveraging events vs uncertainty level
